books.section: Topic 1.6 Cultural Interactions Between Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans
The Early Colonial Era: Spain Colonizes the New World

primary_sources: Hernando Cortes, Second Letter to Charles V (1520), public domain

options.text: The letter was written in Spanish, so its claims could only be checked by Spanish readers.
options.misconception: The language of a source does not decide whether its claims are true.

options.text: Cortes was there in person, so everything he reports about the temple must be reliable.
options.misconception: Being present does not make a writer neutral; Cortes had reason to make his actions look good.

options.text: Cortes writes to justify himself to his king, so he presents his actions as pious.
Cortes describes the temple in detail, which shows the letter is a neutral record.
options.misconception: Detail does not mean neutrality; Cortes chooses what to describe and how.

rationales.general:
1. Ask what the student wants the letter to prove. That Native peoples welcomed Christianity.
2. Look at what the letter actually shows. Cortés imposing images, and the inhabitants objecting.
3. Ask why Cortés wrote it that way. He writes to his king to justify his actions, so he presents them as pious.
4. Name the limit. The letter can prove what Cortés wanted his king to believe, not what the other side felt.
Remember: a source written to justify its author is evidence about the author first, and about others second.
rationales.C: Cortes writes to the king who judges him, so he frames his violence as a holy act. A source written to justify its author must be read with that purpose in mind.
rationales.A: Translation does not fix the problem. The issue is Cortes's purpose, not the language he wrote in.
rationales.B: Eyewitnesses can still mislead. Cortes was present, but he also needed the king to approve of what he did.
rationales.D: A detailed account can still be one-sided. Cortes describes the temple to show his own piety, not to record Native views.

stem: A student wants to use this letter as evidence that Native peoples welcomed Christianity. What is the strongest reason to be careful with that use?

stimulus.source_note: Hernando Cortes, Second Letter to Charles V, October 30, 1520, public domain; quoted in 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 6.
stimulus.text: I precipitated [the idols] from their pedestals, and cast them down the steps of the temple, purifying the chapels in which they had stood, as they were all polluted with human blood, shed in the sacrifices. In the places of these I put images of our Lady and the Saints, which excited not a little feeling in Muteczuma and the inhabitants, who at first remonstrated, declaring that if my proceedings were known throughout the country, the people would rise against me; for they believed that their idols bestowed on them all temporal good, and if they permitted them to be ill-treated, they would be angry and withhold their gifts. ... I answered, through the interpreters, that they were deceived in expecting any favors from idols, the work of their own hands, formed of unclean things; and that they must learn there was but one God, the universal Lord of all, who had created the heavens and earth, and all things else, and had made them and us.
